Storm
storm
n. (a violent disturbance of the air; figuratively, sudden calamity; rendering Hebrew saar and sufah, Greek lailaps)
From the Saxon storm, akin to stir. Hebrew saar is a tempest or whirlwind, from a root meaning to sweep away; the same word describes the whirlwind that took Elijah up and the wind that God rides.

Biblical Definition

A storm in Scripture is never merely weather, because the God who made the wind is always in the sentence. The Psalter states the government plainly: “He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still” (Psalm 107:29) — part of a psalm about men who go down to the sea in ships and see the works of the LORD in the deep. Nahum states the harder half: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3). He is not merely master of the storm; the storm is his road, and the clouds are what his walking kicks up. Isaiah adds the pastoral use: God is “a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall” (Isaiah 25:4) — the storm here being the violence of powerful men, and the shelter being God himself rather than a change in circumstances. Mark records the disciples' night: “there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full” (Mark 4:37), and the Lord was asleep in the hinder part on a pillow. The rebuke he gave was to the wind and then to them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Violent disturbance of the air. Scripture makes God its master, its rider, and the refuge from it — he maketh the storm a calm, has his way in the whirlwind, and is himself the shelter from the blast.

expand to see more

STORM, n. [Sax. storm.] A violent wind; a tempest. Thus a storm of wind, is correct language, as the proper sense of the word is rushing, violence.

2. A violent assault on a fortified place; a furious attempt to take a fort by scaling the walls.

3. Violence; vehemence; tumult; commotion; as a storm of angry passions.

4. Adversity; calamity; distress; affliction.

5. STORM, v.i. To raise a tempest; also, to rage; to be in a violent agitation of passion.

Key Scripture

Psalm 107:29 — "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still."

Nahum 1:3 — "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet."

Isaiah 25:4 — "For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall."

Mark 4:37 — "And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full."

Modern Corruption

God is made the rescuer from storms but not their ruler, so that calamity is treated as outside his government — which spares him blame at the cost of the only comfort actually on offer.

expand to see more

A widespread pastoral instinct, and the formal doctrine of open theism behind much of it, protects God's goodness by limiting his control: he did not send the storm, he only helps in it. The relief is momentary and the cost is total. If the wind is outside his hand, then no promise about it is worth anything, and Psalm 107:29 becomes a hope rather than a fact. Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge and thereby denies the God of Scripture, who declares the end from the beginning and says my counsel shall stand. Nahum 1:3 refuses the escape route in the same breath as it comforts: the LORD is slow to anger, great in power, will not acquit the wicked, and hath his way in the whirlwind. His goodness and his government are asserted together or not at all.

The principle to recover is what happened in the hinder part of the ship. The disciples' question was not canst thou save us but carest thou not that we perish — the accusation was against his love, not his power, which is usually the case. He stilled the wind first and then asked why they were so fearful, how is it that ye have no faith? The storm was not evidence of his indifference; his sleeping in it was evidence of his authority over it, and their terror was a failure to reason from the Person in the boat to the wind outside it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew saar is a tempest or whirlwind, from a root meaning to sweep away; sufah, a storm-wind. Greek lailaps is a squall bursting down, the word of Mark 4:37.

expand to see more

Hebrew saar (H5591) — a tempest, whirlwind; the storm made a calm in Psalm 107:29.

Hebrew sufah (H5492) — a storm-wind, hurricane; they have sown the wind and shall reap the whirlwind.

Hebrew zerem (H2230) — a violent downpour, a storm of rain; the blast against the wall in Isaiah 25:4.

Greek lailaps (G2978) — a squall, a whirlwind bursting down; the great storm on Galilee.

Greek galene (G1055) — a calm; what followed the Lord's rebuke, and it was great.

Usage

"Of God's mastery: he maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still (Psalm 107:29)."

"Of the storm as his road: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm (Nahum 1:3)."

"Of God as the shelter: a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat (Isaiah 25:4)."
